opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think there's one right answer. It shifts depending on where the field is.

Bottom-up is where a lot of the surprising stuff comes from. You give researchers a reasonable slice of compute and the freedom to chase whatever they find interesting, and every so often somebody tries a weird idea that nobody would have approved in a planning meeting, and it turns out to matter. Many of the architectural ideas we now take for granted started as somebody tinkering on the side. If you pull all the compute into a few big centrally planned projects, you lose that. People stop exploring because they can't get the resources to test anything.

The problem is that the most important experiments now are very expensive. You can't find out whether something works at the frontier with a few chips under your desk. Training a big model needs coordination. A lot of people have to agree on one recipe, commit enormous resources, and stop relitigating every decision. That has to be top-down to some degree, or you end up with fifty half-sized projects that each fall short.

So the way I think about it is roughly a portfolio. You want a big, focused bet where the organization has real conviction, and you protect a meaningful chunk of compute for small-scale exploration. Then there's a pipeline between them. Ideas that look promising at small scale get promoted to medium scale. If they keep holding up, they get folded into the big run. A lot of the skill is in that middle layer: figuring out which small results are real and will actually scale, versus which ones are just noise or tricks that only help tiny models.

The other piece is culture. Even when things are top-down, you want researchers to feel ownership. They should be able to argue for their idea and have it judged on evidence rather than on who's pushing it. And you want leadership that understands the technical details well enough to make good calls. Bad top-down allocation is worse than none at all.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier-scale training requires coordination, agreement on one recipe, and committing enormous resources, which supports larger training runs.

r002.rationale: It describes bottom-up exploration as giving researchers compute and freedom, but does not say that adding collaborators increases a project's total compute.

r003.rationale: It discusses centralized projects and a portfolio of research, but does not explain that predefined categories can leave cross-category ideas without resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because I've seen it go both ways. The honest answer is that both approaches have a place, and the failure mode is usually committing too hard to one of them.

The case for bottom-up is that the best ideas in this field have mostly come from people who were just curious and had a few GPUs. Nobody at the top planned the Transformer. It came from a group of people who were annoyed at how slow recurrent models were and wanted to try something. If a committee had been allocating compute by expected value, that project probably wouldn't have gotten much, because it was hard to argue in advance that it would work. So you want some fraction of your compute to be essentially unaccountable. Researchers get it, they do what they think is interesting, and you don't ask too many questions. That's where the surprises come from.

The case for top-down is that at some point the thing you're building gets big enough that no individual can do it alone. Training a frontier model is not a weekend project. You need thousands of chips for months, you need the data pipeline, you need the infrastructure people and the evals people all pointed in the same direction. If you let that be bottom-up, you get twenty half-finished projects and no model. So somebody has to make a call about what the big bet is, and then everyone has to row in that direction even if they personally would have chosen differently.

Where I've seen it break is when organizations treat it as all-or-nothing. If everything is top-down, you get a research lab that's very good at executing on last year's idea and never finds next year's. The people with weird ideas leave, because they can't get resources and they're tired of justifying themselves. If everything is bottom-up, you get a lot of interesting papers and nothing that ships, because nobody can marshal enough compute to actually prove the idea at scale.

My own bias is probably more bottom-up than most people running large efforts, because I've been on the receiving end of it. The small-scale experiment is where you learn the most per dollar. You can try a hundred things at a scale where each one costs almost nothing, and most of them fail, and that's fine. The expensive part is the scale-up, and that's where you want the top-down discipline. So I think about it less as a trade-off and more as a pipeline. Let the bottom-up process generate candidates cheaply. Then use top-down judgment to pick which ones to scale, and be pretty ruthless about that.

The thing I'd add is that the ratio should change over time. Early on, when nobody knows what works, you want to be very bottom-up. Once you have a recipe that clearly works, you want to lean top-down and just scale it. And then eventually the recipe runs out of steam and you need to swing back. The trick is noticing which phase you're in, and most organizations are bad at that. They either stay in exploration mode too long and get beaten by someone who just committed, or they lock in and miss the thing that makes their approach obsolete.

r001.rationale: The response says top-down coordination is needed for frontier training runs requiring thousands of chips for months, clearly connecting it to larger runs.

r002.rationale: It describes bottom-up funding of small experiments, but does not explain that adding collaborators increases a project's total compute resources.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss predefined research categories or explain that cross-category ideas may be left without resources.

astra-6.text:
I think you want some of both. With bottom-up allocation, you give researchers enough compute to try ideas without having to convince the entire organization that they’re right. That’s useful because research is uncertain. If we already knew which experiments were going to work, it wouldn’t be research.

But there are things you can only do with a big, coordinated effort. If everybody has a little slice of the compute, you may never train the large model that would make everybody’s research more useful. That’s where top-down allocation makes sense.

So I’d try to preserve room for lots of small experiments, and then have a way to scale up the promising ones. The tricky part is deciding what counts as promising. You want evidence, but you also want some room for ideas that don’t fit the current recipe. Otherwise you get very good at improving what you already know how to do.

r001.rationale: The response says top-down allocation enables a coordinated effort to train a large model that researchers with smaller compute slices might not be able to train.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that adding collaborators under bottom-up allocation increases a project’s total compute resources.

r003.rationale: It mentions ideas that do not fit the current recipe, but does not explain that predefined research categories can leave cross-category ideas without resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want a mix. Bottom-up allocation is good for discovering things you didn’t know to ask for. Someone has an idea, they run a small experiment, and occasionally it turns out to be much more important than whatever was on the roadmap. If every experiment requires a big organizational decision, you lose a lot of that exploration.

But there are experiments you simply can’t do with spare compute. Training a large model requires coordination and a substantial commitment, so you need some top-down allocation as well.

The useful balance is to make small experiments easy, then have a clear path for promising results to get more resources. And you want to keep questioning those big commitments. Having already spent a lot of compute on something isn’t, by itself, a reason to spend more.
